bullets.text: Machine Learning (ML) is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence (AI).
AI focuses on making machines simulate human intelligence.
ML systems learn patterns from data to make decisions or predictions.
Models improve over time with more data without reprogramming.
It's about teaching computers to learn from experience, not fixed rules.

sections.heading: Ubiquity and Importance of Machine Learning

bullets.text: Machine learning is integrated into many daily technologies.
Examples include Netflix recommendations and email spam filters.
Powers virtual assistants (Siri, Alexa), voice/facial recognition, and fraud detection.
Access to vast amounts of data (social media, web searches, GPS).
Increased computational power, especially with modern GPUs.
Development of sophisticated algorithms for data insight extraction.
Most common type, uses labeled data (input + correct output).
Model learns input-output relationships to predict new outputs.
Example: predicting house prices based on features and past sale prices.
Regression: predicts continuous values (price, temperature).
Classification: predicts discrete labels or categories (spam/not spam).
Uses unlabeled data; goal is to discover patterns or structures independently.
Clustering: groups similar data points, e.g., customer segmentation.
Dimensionality reduction: simplifies data with many features while preserving information (e.g., PCA).
Agent learns by interacting with an environment.
Receives feedback as rewards or penalties for decisions.
Goal: learn a policy to maximize total reward over time.
Examples: training robots to walk, game-playing AI (AlphaGo), self-driving cars.
Supervised learning: learns from labeled data.
Unsupervised learning: finds patterns in unlabeled data.
Reinforcement learning: learns through trial and error with environmental feedback.
Data quality: noisy, biased, or incomplete data degrades model performance.
Overfitting: model learns training data too well, fails on new data.
Ethical concerns: biased data can lead to biased models with real-world consequences.
Understanding data, context, and impact is crucial beyond algorithms.
